bc_recover.text: Release your nose and breathe at your own pace. Take this rest before the second test.

hl_contract.text: If your belly starts to twitch, those are contractions. They're normal. Today, treat them as your signal to stop.

hl_dive2.text: Alongside that urge, your heart may slow as part of the diving response. Humans share this oxygen-conserving response with other mammals.

hl_no_big.text: In the rests, breathe normally. Big or fast breaths before a hold push the urge to breathe back, while your oxygen keeps dropping. That's how people black out.

hl_plan.text: Eight holds, all the same length. The rests get shorter each time, so the urge to breathe tends to come sooner. Your job is to stay relaxed, and to end a hold early whenever you need to.

hl_plan_urge.text: Six holds, no target time. Hold until the first clear urge to breathe, then tap Breathe now. Two minutes of rest between holds. You're learning what a relaxed hold feels like.

hl_recovery2.text: After each hold, let the air out. Then I'll call three recovery breaths: in, a short pause, and out. After those, breathe normally.

hl_rest_why2.text: Breathing between holds lets carbon dioxide fall again. As these rests get shorter, you may start with more, and notice the urge sooner.

hl_rule2.text: Breathe whenever you need to. If you feel dizzy or find yourself straining, stop the table and breathe normally.

ht_cross_intro.text: Core time. Knee across toward the opposite elbow, then back to dog. Right side first.

ht_cross_shoulders.text: When the knee comes in, keep your shoulders over your wrists. Round your upper back a little and push the floor away.

ht_crow_intro.text: Time to play a little. Wrists rest first, in child's pose. Then a squat, with crow if you want it.

ht_crow_lean.text: Look just ahead of your hands. Lean until one foot gets light, maybe both. I'd rather you place them down than hop.

ht_crow_name.text: Baka means crane, kaka means crow. A lot of teachers call the straight-arm version crane and the bent-arm one crow, but the names get mixed up.

ht_crow_set.text: For crow, bring your feet a little closer. Hands shoulder-width, hips up, elbows bent, knees high on your upper arms.

ht_lizard_how.text: Back knee stays down. Hands inside your front foot, or on blocks. Forearms only if your hips settle there without strain.

ht_lizard_press.text: Try a gentle press of the front foot into the floor for three seconds. Let go, take a breath, and see if the stretch eases.

ht_lizard_sink.text: Let your hips lower a little, ribs easy. Stop before your lower back takes over.

ht_plan.text: Core first, then salutations through a squat. Then knee taps, a balance, and a side plank that turns into wild thing. We slow it all down at the end.

ht_rest.text: Let the heat settle. There's nothing to do now.

ht_tap_why.text: Those taps work like a small split squat. Both legs do the work; the front thigh just complains first.

ht_twist.text: Knees rest together, supported if you need it. Keep the opposite shoulder easy; a smaller twist is fine.

kb_a1.text: While you hold, here's what's going on. Your body keeps making carbon dioxide, and with no air moving, it builds up.

kb_a2.text: That rise makes your blood slightly more acidic. Sensors in your brainstem and in your neck pick it up, and the urge builds.

kb_a3.text: At rest, after normal breaths, it's mostly carbon dioxide you feel, not low oxygen. Still, breathe at the first urge.

kb_b1.text: When you breathe again, your heart rate follows the breath. It usually speeds up on the way in and slows on the way out.

kb_b2.text: Slow breathing tends to make that swing bigger, especially around six breaths a minute. A bigger swing doesn't mean you'll feel calmer, though.

kb_b3.text: We're slower than that, and we're adding holds. So don't assume this gives you anything beyond slow breathing on its own.

kb_body.text: Last check: is your whole body braced? Small movements are fine. Only the air needs to pause.

kb_c1.text: The holds also depend on how much air you're holding. With less in your lungs, the urge can arrive sooner.

kb_c2.text: With a full breath you carry more oxygen, and signals from your chest may help hold the urge off a little longer.

kb_c3.text: With practice, holds may feel more familiar. Longer holds don't prove stronger lungs, though. Keep stopping at the urge.

kb_close2.text: Open your eyes when you're ready, and take your time getting up.

kb_even_out.text: Let the air leave evenly, without pushing.

rd_blackout.text: One important thing before we start. If you ever twitch, blank out, or lose track of time in a hold, your brain has run short of oxygen. That's not a release. Stop the session there.

rd_break_1.text: Breathe at your own pace for forty-five seconds before round two.

rd_break_2.text: Another forty-five seconds of ordinary breathing. Let yourself settle before we continue.

rd_break_3.text: No counts for this rest. Take forty-five seconds on your own rhythm.

rd_close.text: Open your eyes whenever you feel ready.

rd_down_rest.text: Before the slower breathing, take a few breaths at your own pace.

rd_how2.text: Fill through your belly and chest, then let the air fall out without pushing.

rd_lead_1.text: We'll take one easy breath in together, then all the way out. The next breath in starts the set.

rd_lead_2.text: One breath in with me, and a full breath out. Then the next set begins.

rd_lead_3.text: Before round three, breathe in together and all the way out. We start again on the next inhale.

rd_lead_4.text: For the last set, one easy breath in, then all the way out. The next inhale starts the faster calls.

rd_oxygen.text: Oxygen can still fall while the urge is delayed. Feeling comfortable, or stopping at the time limit, doesn't guarantee safety.

rd_plan2.text: Four rounds of full breaths, an empty hold, then one recovery breath held for up to fifteen seconds. Breathe whenever you need to; the times are limits, not targets.

rd_quiet2.text: Let the count go and breathe at your own pace for this last minute.

rd_study_comparison.text: Slower practices helped too. That study doesn't establish a benefit from these longer empty holds, or a reason to push them.

rd_study2.text: With that limit in mind, one month-long study found improved mood and less anxiety after five daily minutes of fast breathing with short holds.

rd_t_relax.text: Let your shoulders drop and your hands go soft.

rd_tap.text: Whenever you need to breathe, tap Breathe now.

rd_tingle2.text: Fast breathing can cause tingling or lightheadedness. If that happens, slow down or breathe normally.

rd_welcome.text: Hey. Sit or lie down somewhere comfortable, where you can't fall. Never near water with this one.

rd_why2.text: The fast breaths lowered carbon dioxide, which usually drives the urge to breathe. That can delay the urge during the empty hold.

ready_before_box.text: Take a few ordinary breaths before the box.

ready_before_even.text: Stay with your own breathing for a few seconds. Then an easier pace.

ready_before_hum.text: Let your breathing find its own pace before the hums.

ready_between.text: Breathe at your own pace here, low into your belly.

ready_first2.text: Open your eyes and breathe freely. Picture the first thing you'll do or say.

ready_hum.text: Three hums. Lips closed, teeth apart, and hum at an easy pitch on the way out. It warms up your voice.

ready_lead.text: Breathe in together, then all the way out. Next breath starts the box.

ready_permission.text: Breathe whenever you need to. Stay seated for the holds, and never practise them in water.

ready_plan_desk2.text: Sit tall, feet flat, eyes on one spot.

ready_plan_stage2.text: Sit tall. We finish with three hums for your voice.

ready_plan_start2.text: Stand easy, eyes open. No holds before a start.

ready_settle.text: A few slow breaths may help you settle before you start.

ready_sigh.text: Two sighs. Breathe in through your nose, top it up with a second short sniff, then let it all go slowly through your mouth.

ready_why2.text: Your heart usually slows a little on the breath out.

reps_breath2.text: Breathe at your own pace for a few moments before counting. There's no rhythm to follow.

reps_check.text: Notice how your head feels now, compared to when you sat down. It might be busy, clear, or somewhere in between. Any of that's fine.

reps_close.text: Open your eyes. Go do the first thing on your list.

reps_plan2.text: Count each out-breath silently, from one to ten, then start over. If you lose track, begin at one again. We're practising noticing when attention drifts.

reps_release2.text: Let the counting go now. Keep breathing at your own pace while you sit here for a bit.

reps_t_drift2.text: If a thought takes over, you don't have to finish it before bringing your attention back to the breath.

reps_t_quiet2.text: Keep each number brief in your head, so you can still notice the breath it's counting.

reps_welcome.text: Morning. Sit up, comfortable but awake. Hands on your thighs, and close your eyes.

reps_why_limits.text: That study involved much longer sits than this. It doesn't tell us whether a few minutes will improve focus at work.

reps_why2.text: Researchers use breath counting to study mindful attention. In one study, people counted more accurately after several weeks of practice.

res_close.text: Open your eyes when you like. Ten minutes a day is a good start, and more is fine if you enjoy it.

res_find_plan.text: This is a pace test. Five slow paces, two minutes each, with a minute of normal breathing in between. After each one, notice how it felt: smooth and easy, hungry for air, or lightheaded. If a pace makes you lightheaded, stop following it and just breathe.

res_gadget_1.text: That swing is called heart rate variability.

res_gadget_2.text: One study had people breathe at six a minute.

res_gadget_3.text: Some had a heart-rate monitor to follow, some didn't.

res_gadget_4.text: Their variability rose about the same either way.

res_gadget_5.text: So you don't need a monitor for this.

res_interval.text: A few breaths at your own pace before we settle into the main rhythm.

res_light.text: If you feel lightheaded, make the breaths smaller, or stop following the pace for a bit.

res_pick2.text: Breathe freely now. Pick the pace that felt smoothest, without straining or feeling lightheaded. Choose it above the Begin button next time. Test again in a few weeks, because it can shift.

res_plan.text: This is resonance breathing: slow, easy breaths at one steady pace, for about ten minutes. No holds.

res_quiet2.text: Only the breath calls from here.

res_rate_2b.text: Let the counts go for this rest. Remember whether that pace felt easy or strained.

res_rate_3b.text: Back to ordinary breathing. Notice how that one sat with you before we slow down again.

res_rate_4b.text: Another minute without counts. Keep that pace in mind. One more to go, the slowest.

res_rate2.text: Breathe at your own pace for a minute. Was that pace smooth, hungry for air, or lightheaded? Remember it.

res_return.text: Let the pace go, and breathe on your own.

res_slower.text: At these slower paces, keep the breaths small and easy.

res_small.text: Slow doesn't mean big. Keep each breath small and smooth.

res_t_nose2.text: Use your nose if it's easy.

res_t_wander2.text: Bring your attention to this exhale.

res_waves_1.text: Your heart rate is following your breathing right now.

res_waves_3.text: And now it's slowing down again.

res_waves_4.text: Slow breathing makes that swing bigger.

res_waves_5.text: With practice, some studies find less stress.

res_welcome.text: Welcome. Sit back, let your hands rest, and close your eyes.

st_close2.text: Let the pace go now. Give your breathing time to settle before you get up.

st_plan.text: We'll do ten tiny holds. A small breath out, a short pause, then quiet breathing. If a pause ever feels like too much, skip it and just breathe gently.

st_pull2.text: If you need more air, take it. Leave out the next pause if your breathing needs time to settle.

st_recover.text: The holds are finished. Take a few breaths at your own pace before the slower rhythm.

st_safety.text: If you have chest pain, or an asthma attack your inhaler isn't helping, stop here and get help instead.

st_settle.text: Breathe at your own pace for a little while. You can breathe whenever you need to during a pause, too.

st_small2.text: We'll take one small breath in and a normal breath out together first. The next breath begins the holds. Don't push the air out.

st_t_jaw.text: Check your jaw while you rest. Let your teeth part if they're pressed together.

st_t_soft.text: Between holds, let your shoulders drop and your belly go soft.

st_welcome2.text: Hey. Sit or lie down, away from water. Breathe gently through your nose if that's easy.

st_why_1.text: When breathing moves more air than your body needs, carbon dioxide can fall.

st_why_2.text: That fall can contribute to dizziness or tingling. Those symptoms can have other causes too.

st_why_3.text: Gentler breathing may let carbon dioxide return toward its usual level. These pauses should stay easy.

tw_after_middle_hum.text: Take a few ordinary breaths before the last round.

tw_before_hum.text: Leave the counts here. Breathe naturally while I explain the humming.

tw_checkin2.text: Let your breathing find its own pace. Notice how you're doing; we'll stay here for a minute.

tw_close2.text: Have something warm to drink if you like. If a fever turns up, skip the rounds and rest. Take your time getting up.

tw_co2_1.text: While you pause, carbon dioxide builds again. Fast breathing lowers it without adding much oxygen, because blood oxygen is usually already near full at rest.

tw_co2_2.text: That drop can cause tingling or lightness. As carbon dioxide rises again, it usually drives the urge to breathe more than falling oxygen does.

tw_co2_3.text: So after fast breathing, the urge can arrive late while oxygen keeps falling. A comfortable hold is still no guarantee of safety. Breathe before you need to strain.

tw_co2_gentle.text: Unlike these slow breaths, fast breathing lowers carbon dioxide without adding much oxygen. Blood oxygen is usually already near full at rest. During a hold, carbon dioxide builds again.

tw_easy.text: There are no holds at this level. Breathe at your own pace whenever the counts don't suit you.

tw_first.text: Keep the first breath after a hold calm. If you gasped, hold a bit less next time.

tw_hum_again2.text: Another set of three hums now, starting with the breath in.

tw_hum_how2.text: We'll do three hums. Breathe in through your nose, then hum all the way out with lips closed and teeth slightly apart. Keep it low.

tw_hum_last.text: Three last hums. Long and low.

tw_hum_rest.text: Breathe at your own pace again while we rest.

tw_hum_space.text: The first hum released the most. Another study found the boost came back after three quiet minutes, which is why the hums are spaced out. It doesn't make humming a cold treatment.

tw_hum_why2.text: Humming moves sinus air into the nose, releasing nitric oxide. A small study measured fifteen times more during humming than a quiet exhale.

tw_kox_1.text: Those changes were studied in healthy young men in 2014. They trained for ten days with fast breathing, holds, cold exposure and meditation.

tw_kox_2.text: After that training, researchers injected a bacterial toxin that causes brief flu-like symptoms. The trained men released more adrenaline, had less inflammation, and reported feeling less sick.

tw_kox_3.text: But that was a small study of healthy people, and the toxin wasn't a virus. It suggests an effect on the immune response, not that these rounds treat a cold.

tw_ladder2.text: We'll lengthen the breath gradually. Start with four in, four out. I'll call each change.

tw_last_rest.text: Breathe freely again for a bit. Then we'll finish with humming.

tw_lead_1.text: One breath together first. The next breath in starts round one.

tw_lead_2.text: In with me, all the way out, then into round two.

tw_lead_3.text: One easy breath first; the next inhale starts our last round.

tw_lock2.text: During a full hold, gently lift your pelvic floor and lower your chin if that stays easy.

tw_nh_1.text: No hold follows. Breathe at your own pace until I call the next round.

tw_nh_2.text: Leave the rhythm now and take some ordinary breaths before we hum again.

tw_nh_3.text: The slow rounds are done. Take a little uncounted breathing before the cool-down.

tw_nose_why2.text: The nose warms, moistens and filters incoming air. The sinuses also produce nitric oxide, which is involved in airway defenses. Mouth breathing bypasses that nasal conditioning.

tw_nose2.text: Use your nose if it's comfortable. Keep the breathing quiet, without forcing it.

tw_permission.text: Never do this in water. Breathe at the first urge, or sooner; Breathe now ends a hold. Stop if you're dizzy or unwell.

tw_r1_2.text: Round one uses short, sharp breaths out through the nose, from the belly. Let each breath in happen by itself. Keep your face relaxed.

tw_r2_2.text: Round two has more breaths and a longer empty hold. End it early if that's enough today.

tw_r3.text: Last round. Let it be the easiest one.

tw_rest_1.text: Let the air out. Take twenty seconds of breathing at your own pace before the next round.

tw_rest_2.text: Release the breath and return to normal breathing. Take this whole rest before the next hums.

tw_rest_3.text: Let it go. Breathe without counts for a bit before the cool-down.

tw_ribs.text: As you breathe in, let your ribs widen out to the sides. Shoulders stay where they are, belly soft.

tw_sleep.text: Short sleep was also linked to catching colds, especially under six hours a night. That doesn't mean this session prevents one. Give yourself time to rest tonight.

tw_stay.text: Stay where you are for a minute before you get up. After holds, standing up fast can make you dizzy.

tw_stress.text: Slow breathing may help with stress. In studies where volunteers were exposed to cold viruses, people reporting more stress were more likely to get sick.

tw_t_ears.text: If you like, rest your thumbs lightly on the little flaps at the front of your ears. The hum may sound louder inside your head.

tw_t_slower2.text: If the quick breaths took effort, use normal breathing for the next round.

tw_vagus2.text: Your heart often slows a little on the out-breath.

tw_welcome.text: Hey. Rough day? Let's look after you a bit. Sit up tall, or lie down if that's easier, and close your eyes.

ws_break_1.text: Breathe at your own pace before the second pause.

ws_break_2.text: Let your breathing settle on its own rhythm now.

ws_break_3.text: No counts here. Take a few ordinary breaths.

ws_break_4.text: Breathe normally for a bit before the last pause.

ws_break_5.text: The pauses are done. Rest on your own breathing.

ws_brow.text: Let your forehead go smooth. Soften around your eyes, and across your scalp.

ws_checkin.text: Notice how your head and jaw feel now. If something has eased, let it stay that way.

ws_close.text: That's it. Have some water. If the headache keeps going or gets worse, get it checked out. Come back to this whenever you need it.

ws_face_why.text: Your jaw, forehead and shoulders often tighten up around a headache. Letting them go may take off some of the pressure.

ws_h_brow.text: Let your forehead soften, and the muscles around your eyes.

ws_h_hands.text: Let your hands get heavy in your lap.

ws_h_jaw.text: Let your jaw hang soft. Teeth apart.

ws_h_last.text: Last pause. Breathe whenever you like, even before the cue.

ws_h_sway.text: On a train, let it rock you a little instead of bracing.

ws_jaw.text: Lips together, teeth apart. Let your tongue rest on the floor of your mouth.

ws_lead.text: One easy breath in together, then all the way out. The next breath in starts the first pause.

ws_long_rest.text: Let the counts go for a bit and breathe normally before we finish.

ws_long_why.text: A longer breath out gives your heart more time to slow down.

ws_neck.text: If it's comfortable, let the back of your neck get long, with your chin tipped down a little.

ws_pain_limit.text: Whether that carries over to headaches hasn't been tested.

ws_pain_out.text: The long out-breath seemed to matter most.

ws_pain2.text: In one lab study, slow breathing eased heat pain a little.

ws_pause_intro2.text: Now a few soft pauses with a relaxed throat, without pushing. Stay seated, and never practise holds in water. Breathe whenever you need to.

ws_release2.text: Back to four in, six out. Gentle neck tilts next, if comfortable. You can keep your head still.

ws_shoulders.text: Every time you breathe out, let your shoulders drop a little more.

ws_silent.text: Everything here is silent. Nose only, small breaths. Nobody around you needs to know.

ws_skip.text: If the throbbing gets worse, or your head feels fuller, skip the pauses for today and just make the breath out longer.

ws_small.text: Slower, not bigger. Big breaths can make you lightheaded.

ws_stress_limit.text: Calmer breathing might help, but it's unproven.

ws_stress_time.text: And one session wouldn't show it either way.

ws_stress2.text: And stress can push inflammation up.

ws_t_anchor2.text: Notice the air moving at your nostrils.

ws_t_shoulders2.text: Let your shoulders drop if they've crept up.

ws_t_sounds2.text: Let the sounds around you stay in the background.

ws_t_wander2.text: If you lose track, follow this breath out.

ws_t_window2.text: With eyes open, you can let the view pass.

ws_tilt_r2.text: Gently tip your head toward your right shoulder.

ws_transition.text: Breathe at your own pace for twenty seconds before the next part.

ws_vagal_limit.text: The same nerve is involved in inflammation.

ws_vagal2.text: Your heart also tends to slow on each out-breath.

ws_vagus.text: That change runs through the vagus nerve.

ws_welcome.text: Hey. Sit back, with your head on the headrest if you can, and your feet flat on the floor. Eyes down, or closed. If you've got water, take a sip now.

yg_back_rock.text: Rock a little side to side if your lower back likes it.

yg_by_ear2.text: You can put the phone down. I'll call every move, and which side. If my pace doesn't match your breath, go with your breath. I won't mind.

yg_child_history2.text: Exercise versions of sun salutations were promoted in the 1920s and thirties. The sun worship is far older, and the flowing sequences we do today have changed since.

yg_child_knees2.text: Knees wide or together, whichever lets your hips settle.

yg_close2.text: That's the flow. Roll onto your side when you're ready, and take your time sitting up. Nice work today.

yg_dog_hands2.text: Spread your fingers wide and keep the whole palm on the mat, so you're not tipping onto the outer edge of your hands.

yg_dog_pedal2.text: Take a few breaths here. Pedal it out, one knee, then the other. No rush.

yg_dog_serratus2.text: Pushing the floor away recruits serratus anterior, among others. It holds your shoulder blades against your ribs, and you want it in every plank today.

yg_hips2.text: Hips next. Pigeon, both sides. If your front knee complains at any point, come out.

yg_hm_balance2.text: Balance runs on your eyes, your inner ear, and your sense of where your body is. A steady spot on the floor helps; look up, and you change that reference.

yg_hm_stack2.text: Let the top hip open, flex the lifted foot, and keep your gaze down.

yg_hm_wobble.text: Wobbling is fine. Your standing foot is making lots of small corrections, and that's the training.

yg_lunge_ribs2.text: Reach up without flaring the ribs. I think of zipping up a jacket.

yg_lunge_shape2.text: Back heel reaches back, back knee lifts. Front knee right over your ankle.

yg_pigeon_belly.text: Let your belly soften on each breath out.

yg_pigeon_prep2.text: Technically this is the prep. Full pigeon, eka pada rajakapotasana, adds a deep backbend, with the back foot reaching for your head.

yg_pigeon_rotators2.text: Piriformis gets all the credit, but several muscles share the work around your hip. Your hip angle changes how they're loaded.

yg_pigeon_set2.text: Back leg long, top of the foot down. A cushion under your front hip if it floats.

yg_pigeon_square2.text: Let your hips face forward without forcing them. Support the front hip if that helps.

yg_pigeon_stretch2.text: A stretch can give you a little more range for now. Regular practice builds that range over time, partly by changing how much stretch you tolerate.

yg_plan2.text: We'll wake up the spine, then build one flow, a piece at a time. Right side, then left, every round. Then hips, a twist, and rest.

yg_r1b.text: Round one is simple: into a lunge, and back. Right side first.

yg_r2b.text: Round two. Same start, then warrior two. I'll call the feet as we go.

yg_r3c.text: Last round, and half moon joins in. Keep your block close.

yg_rest_text2.text: Savasana's coming up. It's one of only about fifteen poses in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a fifteenth-century text, and most of the others are seated.

yg_rest2.text: Let go of the breath count. Just breathe.

yg_twist_liver2.text: Twists rotate your spine. They don't wring toxins out of your liver; your liver handles that with enzymes, no squeezing required.

yg_twist_ribs.text: Let the breath widen the ribs on the open side.

yg_twist_shoulder2.text: Let the opposite shoulder settle. If it lifts, keep your knees a little higher. Turn your head only if your neck likes it.

yg_w2_burn.text: Thighs talking to you yet? Mine usually start about now.

yg_w2_knee2.text: Front knee tracks over your middle toes. Shoulders stay right above your hips.

yg_w2_name.text: The warriors are named for Virabhadra, a fierce warrior in a story about Shiva. Some teachers read warrior one, two and three as his fight, in order.

yg_welcome3.text: Hey. This one's a short flow, about fifteen minutes. Grab a block or a cushion if you have one, and sit at the back of your mat.
